blocks.text: Permissions are checked by numeric UID/GID; a bind mount exposes host files with host ownership unchanged, so container users that don't match can't write, and root containers leave root-owned files on the host.

rows: Container UID 10001, host dir owned by 1000, mode 755
Container runs as root, writes into mount
Root-owned files on host; your editor/git can't modify them

blocks.text:
$ ls -ln ./data
drwxr-xr-x 2 1000 1000 4096 ./data
$ docker run --rm -u 10001 -v "$PWD/data:/data" alpine touch /data/x
touch: /data/x: Permission denied

items: Use a named volume if you don't edit the files on the host (the image decides ownership).
Dev: run as your UID: `-u "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` or `user: "${UID}:${GID}"` (set HOME=/tmp if needed).
Build with a matching UID (`ARG UID=1000`).
chown the host dir to the container UID for data you don't edit.
Rootless Docker / userns-remap for UID mapping.

blocks.text: `chmod -R 777` makes the data writable by every user and process on the host. Don't.
Docker Desktop hides UID mismatches through its file-sharing layer, so setups pass on a Mac and fail on Linux CI. SELinux hosts may also need `:z`/`:Z` relabeling.

Q: "A non-root container gets permission denied on a bind mount. Why and how do you fix it?" A: "The kernel compares numeric UIDs; the host directory belongs to a different UID. Use a named volume, run the container with the host user's UID in dev, or chown the directory to the container UID. Never 777."
